source_emails.subject: Suggested Corrections for Psalms (Part I)
preamble: The transcription of Merekha and Meteg from L into the UXLC is challenging, as the image often looks like a Meteg while UXLC reads it as a Merekha, and vice versa. Many of these Merekhas appear to be carryovers from the BHS. While each word should follow an accent rule, I understand your goal is to transcribe exactly what the image of L shows regarding the slant of the vertical mark. To ensure we are aligned, I can continue tracking these occurrences throughout the rest of the Bible. Let me know your thoughts!
Below is the first part of Psalms, broken down to keep the email size manageable with the attached images.

fields.label: Suggested Correction

fields.label: Critical Note
fields.value: Going by appearance, this mark does not look like a Mereka due to its slant. Dotan has a Munach. This word is in the domain of Zaqef Qatan, and the servant of Zaqef Qatan is always Munach. Price noted BHS and BHK erroneously have Mereka, which is possibly a defect in L (Page 65, Syntax of Masoretic Accents).

fields.label: Suggested Correction
fields.value: Change Meteg to Mercha OR include an apparatus note detailing the manuscript variants.

fields.label: Critical Note
fields.value: Dotan features a Mercha. In Daat Miqra, Breuer reads both Aleppo (A) and Leningrad (L) as having a Mercha. Conversely, Sassoon 1053 and Jacob ben Chayyim print a Meteg, but crucially include a Maqqef to bind the word to the subsequent Silluq. If the Meteg tradition is maintained, an editorial note should indicate that alternate manuscripts require a Maqqef; an independent word cannot sit accentless directly preceding a Silluq without violating Tiberian accentuation syntax.
